Four challenges show up at scale, beyond the obvious "you need to version events".

- **Replay performance.** An aggregate with millions of events takes too long to rebuild on every load. The fix is periodic snapshots: store the derived state every N events, then replay only the events since the last snapshot. You also need a plan for invalidating snapshots when your aggregate logic changes.

worst_places.quote: Kafka's exactly-once guarantee is built from two separate mechanisms working together, and understanding what each one actually does (and doesn't) is the difference between using it correctly and assuming more than it delivers.
worst_places.problem: event-driven-q-22 (en, and identically in ru). The question asks how exactly-once is achieved. The first sentence of the answer announces that there are two mechanisms and then spends the rest of its 34 words on why understanding them matters — it never names them. worst_places.before: Kafka's exactly-once guarantee is built from two separate mechanisms working together, and understanding what each one actually does (and doesn't) is the difference between using it correctly and assuming more than it delivers.
worst_places.after: Kafka gets exactly-once from two separate mechanisms: an idempotent producer (which kills duplicates caused by producer retries) and transactions (which make a write and a consumer offset commit atomic together). Each solves a different problem, and knowing which is which is the difference between using them correctly and assuming more than they deliver.

worst_places.quote:
const alreadyProcessed = await redis.set(dedupKey, '1', { NX: true, EX: 259200 }); // 72h TTL, atomic check-and-set
  if (!alreadyProcessed) return; // duplicate within the retention window
worst_places.problem: event-driven-q-20 (en and ru). The variable name says the opposite of what it holds: `redis.set(..., { NX: true })` returns a truthy value when the key did *not* exist, i.e. when the event was **not** already processed. So `alreadyProcessed` is truthy exactly when it hasn't been processed, and `if (!alreadyProcessed) return` returns on a duplicate — correct behaviour, backwards name. A reader who trusts the name reads the guard as inverted and concludes the example is broken. Worse, the comment three lines below admits the whole snippet is the anti-pattern the answer's pitfall section warns against ("real systems set the dedup key AFTER successful processing"), so the one code example in the entry demonstrates the wrong approach.

worst_places.before: CRUD uses one model and usually one schema for both reading and writing — simple to reason about, but it forces every read to go through the same normalized shape that writes need for integrity, which means joins, indexes tuned as a compromise, and a single point of scaling for both traffic patterns.
worst_places.after: CRUD (create, read, update, delete — the plain "one table, one model" style) uses a single model and usually a single schema for both reading and writing. So you get joins, indexes tuned as a compromise between the two, and one single point of scaling for both traffic patterns.

worst_places.quote: What concretely breaks each mode, in Avro/Protobuf terms: adding a field is backward-compatible only if it has a default value (old-schema readers simply don't know about it, but new-schema readers processing old data will use the default); removing a field is forward-compatible only if it had a default (so new-schema readers don't choke on its absence) — removing a field with no default breaks anyone still expecting it; renaming a field is effectively "remove old name + add new name" and breaks compatibility unless the format supports field aliases;

worst_places.before: What concretely breaks each mode, in Avro/Protobuf terms: adding a field is backward-compatible only if it has a default value (old-schema readers simply don't know about it, but new-schema readers processing old data will use the default); removing a field is forward-compatible only if it had a default (so new-schema readers don't choke on its absence) — removing a field with no default breaks anyone still expecting it; renaming a field is effectively "remove old name + add new name" and breaks compatibility unless the format supports field aliases;
worst_places.after:
Here is what concretely breaks each mode, in Avro/Protobuf terms.

- **Adding a field** is backward-compatible only if the field has a default value. Old-schema readers simply don't know about it; new-schema readers processing old data fall back to the default.
- **Removing a field** is forward-compatible only if that field had a default, so new-schema readers don't choke on its absence. Remove a field with no default and you break everyone still expecting it.
- **Renaming a field** is really "remove the old name, add the new one". It breaks compatibility unless the format supports field aliases.

The items are already separate thoughts — the same file uses real markdown bullets correctly in q-1 and q-15, so this is a habit, not a constraint.

The single code example always sits at the very end, after all the theory, and in the hardest entries it illustrates the easiest part of the answer rather than the part that needed anchoring: q-15 gives three broker-comparison paragraphs then a snippet about seeking an offset; q-21 defines four compatibility modes and four breaking changes then shows only the safe additive case; q-12 lists four scaling challenges then shows snapshot loading, which was challenge (1). The dense middle of each answer has nothing to hold on to.

Acronyms are spelled out in the one entry that happens to introduce them and used bare everywhere else — CQRS is expanded once, in q-5's question text, then used unexplained in q-9, q-10, q-12 and q-18; CRUD is never expanded in either locale. A question bank is read one card at a time in random order, so per-entry expansion is the only expansion that counts.

The RU text is broadly living Russian, but breaks into transliteration exactly where the English term is a verb: «ключуйте» (key by), «истекайте записи» (expire entries), «переретраенное сообщение» (retried), «переразмеренный/недоразмеренный агрегат» (oversized/undersized), «просто в осмыслении» (simple to reason about). Nouns get borrowed cleanly; verbs get mangled.

EN is measurably harder than RU (6896 vs 6190 words, 73.8% vs 62.6% long sentences), which is the reverse of what the ~19% expansion rule would predict as merely borderline; the EN register also leans idiomatic ("papers the wall", "poison message", "buys you nothing", "a tax you pay on every deploy").
